_comment: USER-FACING highlights for the release named by `version`, published to the website as
part of https://devicechain.io/releases.json (see hack/build-release-manifest.sh).
🔴 UPDATE THIS IN THE PR THAT PREPARES A RELEASE, BEFORE TAGGING — and update `version`,
`theme`, `breaking` and `highlights` TOGETHER. They are one record of one release, and
the way this file goes wrong is three of the four moving while the fourth keeps last
release's answer: a theme naming work that is not in the highlights below it reads as
confidently as one that is. The `guard` job fails
the release when `version` does not match the tag, deliberately and as the FIRST job —
so a forgotten update costs nothing but a re-run, rather than publishing last release's
highlights against this release's version. Confidently wrong is worse than absent, and
this file is the one part of the manifest a machine cannot derive.
`theme` IS THE ONE PHRASE THAT NAMES THE RELEASE — a chapter title, not a changelog
line. It leads the GitHub release notes and it reaches releases.json, so it is the
first thing a reader decides against. A good one names what changed about the system:
"the instance is declared, not remembered". A bad one is a category ("bug fixes and
improvements"), the version restated, or the first highlight with its verbs filed off —
if it would fit any release, it is not this release's theme.
Write a PHRASE. The guard caps it at 72 characters, the width of a commit subject,
because past that you are writing a sentence, and a sentence about what changed is a
highlight — there is already a list for those below. The cap is the only taste this
file can enforce; the rest is on you.
🔴 The theme is PUBLISHED, and so is every highlight — into the GitHub release body and
into devicechain.io/releases.json. No ADR references in either: ADRs live in a repo the
reader cannot open, so a citation is a dead reference dressed as a source. Say the thing
itself, or link to a public page. THIS BLOCK IS DIFFERENT — `_comment` is published
nowhere, it is the only part of the file a reader never sees, and it may cite ADR-080 or
any other freely. The guard reads exactly that distinction: it scans `theme` and
`highlights[]`, case-insensitively, and leaves this block alone.
WRITE FOR SOMEONE DECIDING WHETHER TO UPGRADE, not for someone reading the commit log.
The changelog is already generated from commit subjects and is right there in the release
notes; repeating `fix(events): give payload rows and anchors identities of their own` here
adds nothing. Say what changed for the person running the platform.
Keep it to a handful of lines. This renders in the website's download menu, not in a
document — a fifteen-item list is a changelog wearing a different hat.
`breaking` MEANS 'THIS RELEASE HAS BREAKING CHANGES'. It does NOT mean 'you must recreate
your instance', and this comment used to say it did — it told you to set the flag when an
upgrade is not a plain `helm upgrade`. The website has not read it that way since the
copy was repaired: `true` renders exactly one sentence, 'This release has breaking changes
— read the release notes before upgrading', and `false` renders nothing at all. So set it
true whenever something breaks for SOMEBODY — an API caller, an operator, a package
consumer — and use the first highlight to say who, and whether the upgrade itself is
ordinary. If a release ever genuinely requires recreating an instance, give that its OWN
manifest field rather than overloading this one a second time.
The other correction: there is no docs banner. Nothing under docs/ fetches releases.json.
The website download menu is this file's only consumer.
For each highlight, ask whether it makes a sentence on the marketing site stale. The
site is a separate repository and nothing here reads its prose. Answering "no site
impact" is a fine answer; not asking is not.
theme: instances stop owning the cluster they run on
highlights: There is no in-place upgrade into this release. Every instance built by v0.16.0 or earlier recorded no declaration of what it is -- the record an upgrade now reads to know what to deploy -- so it must be destroyed and built again, and with the current dcctl the cluster is rebuilt too, not just the instance. `dcctl upgrade` refuses and prints the recipe rather than doing anything partial. Export first: the destroy guard protects the databases from an ordinary helm operation, not from a deliberate `dcctl destroy`, and there is no in-place path that preserves your telemetry, device definitions or dashboards across this release.

`dcctl bootstrap` is now two commands. `dcctl install <provider>` prepares a CLUSTER -- the shared relational store, the operator and its CRDs, cert-manager, the monitoring stack -- and `dcctl bootstrap <provider> <instance>` builds an instance on a cluster that is already prepared. Everything that sizes or shapes the cluster moved to `install` and is recorded there, so `--ha`, `--compact`, `--no-monitoring`, `--no-cnpg` and `--max-connections` are set once and every instance on that cluster follows them; a bootstrap has no flags for them any more. `dcctl destroy` now tears down one instance's own infrastructure and leaves the cluster standing.

One cluster holds as many instances as you build. Each gets a namespace of its own -- `dci-<instance>`, not the bare instance name -- with its own broker, its own event store, and its own login and database in the shared relational store. Every `kubectl` command you have written down against an instance needs the prefix. Two things are still one-per-cluster and are claimed by whichever instance takes them first: the ingress host and, on a local cluster, the MQTT NodePort. A second instance asking for a host another instance serves is refused before anything is written.

A bootstrap now asks the relational store what it already holds before it mints a root key. A database sitting there under the instance's name can only have outlived the cluster that built it, so the bootstrap stops instead of sealing recovered rows under a fresh key that will never open them -- the failure that previously reported success and left every stored secret permanently unreadable. Two consequences for recovery: it has to use the instance's original name, and `--restore-root-key` is accepted only where there is something for the key to open. `dcctl install` gained `--restore-rdb-from` and `--restore-rdb-at` so the shared relational store is recovered as the cluster is built.

If you grant `dcctl` explicit RBAC on a cluster somebody else administers, it needs verbs it did not before: `list`, `patch` and `delete` on `instances.core.devicechain.io` alongside `get`, `create` and `update`, plus `list` on secrets in `dc-system`. Every bootstrap and upgrade now asks the cluster which instances it already holds and what they have claimed, and that question is a list. An account holding only the previously documented set is refused partway through a bootstrap.

Grafana single sign-on through DeviceChain is gone. Grafana is reached by port-forwarding its Service -- there is no ingress route -- and signed into with a per-cluster admin credential in the `dc-grafana-admin` Secret, which now survives `dcctl install` re-runs instead of being rotated by each one. Each instance gets its own dashboard folder. Note that hand-editing that Secret does not rotate the password: Grafana reads it at start-up, so the Secret and the running server disagree silently until the Deployment restarts.

dcctl's local state moved. Per-instance records are under `~/.devicechain/instances/<instance>/`, and a new per-cluster directory `~/.devicechain/clusters/<cluster-uid>/` holds the cluster's own infrastructure state -- the only copy, in no backup, and the reason `dcctl install` can only be re-run from the machine that installed the cluster. This release's dcctl deliberately does not read the older layout, so `dcctl instances list` will not show instances built by v0.16.0 or earlier; they are still in their clusters, and `helm list -A` still shows their releases.
